details:
Summary

I built the Martian Map, a browser tool that layers NASA Mars data for planning a surface excursion. The layers are Viking optical imagery, MOLA elevation, THEMIS infrared, a high-resolution Context Camera mosaic of Gale Crater, and USGS geologic units. In mission mode, the user steps through four stops on Curiosity’s route from Bradbury Landing to Murray Buttes and sees each stop’s coordinates, the distance and walking time from the last one, and a rover photo of the place. A route planner measures distance and walking time between clicked waypoints at an adjustable pace, and a radiation card gives the doses Curiosity measured.

The challenge asks for a layered, local view that helps a human explorer plan a Marswalk. This project brings optical, thermal, topographic and geologic data together at the scale of one traverse, with radiation context for crew safety. It is a prototype: routes are straight lines, and there is no slope or hazard layer yet.

Astronauts will have to plan each excursion around terrain, distance and radiation, and NASA’s data is not yet layered together for that kind of local planning.

What it does and how it works

The basemap is the Viking color mosaic. Users can switch on MOLA elevation, THEMIS infrared, a Context Camera mosaic of Gale Crater, and USGS geologic units. Mission mode follows four stops on Curiosity’s route, each with coordinates, distance and walking time from the previous stop, a source link and a rover photo. The route planner takes clicked waypoints and reports total distance and walking time at an adjustable pace, 2 km/h by default. Distance uses the haversine formula on Mars’ mean radius of 3,389.5 km. A radiation card gives Curiosity’s measured doses. Six sites, including Jezero Crater and Olympus Mons, open from a dropdown with a popup that links their NASA source.

Benefits

The terrain, thermal, geologic and radiation information a crew would want sits in one view at the scale of a single traverse. Each stop shows what the place looks like in a real rover photo. Every figure links to a NASA or USGS page, so a user can check where it came from. The tool runs in a current browser with nothing to install.

Intended impact

The project shows how a layered, local map could support planning a Marswalk, where today the data is spread across tools built for regional and global views. It is a prototype and not a navigation system. The sites and stops are plain data in the code, so adding a location means adding entries, though only Gale has a high-resolution overlay so far.

Tools and technologies

The app is one HTML file with CSS and JavaScript, built with Leaflet 1.9.4 and no build step. Data comes from NASA Mars Trek map tiles and the USGS Geologic Map of Mars (Tanaka et al., 2014), served through ArcGIS. I used Git and GitHub for version control. I worked alone and used Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant, to help write and review the code, check sources, and draft the README and submission text. I reviewed and tested the results myself. No special hardware is needed.

Creativity

Mars Trek and the USGS map are built for global and regional browsing. This project uses the same data at a much smaller scale and adds what someone on foot needs: distance, walking time, a photo of the destination and a radiation reference. Mission mode turns Curiosity’s real route into a short guided traverse, so a user can see how a surface plan would read.

Factors considered

The challenge puts astronaut safety first, so radiation is included, though as a reference card and not a map layer. I used only NASA and USGS sources, cited all of them, and removed figures I couldn’t trace to NASA. The geologic map is regional at 1:20,000,000, so the app warns users when they zoom in close. A notice appears when a layer’s tiles fail to load. I kept the scope to one location, Gale Crater, in one self-contained file. Routes are straight lines, and there is no slope, hazard or live space-weather data yet. The original work is open source under the MIT License, and Leaflet is BSD-2-Clause.
